hints: Start by asking what burning sulfur in excess oxygen actually makes first, and what still needs to happen to get to $\text{SO}_3$.
Remember that $\text{NO}_2$ is a good oxidising agent that can turn $\text{SO}_2$ into $\text{SO}_3$ while itself being reduced to $\text{NO}$.
Consider what happens to $\text{NO}$ when excess oxygen is present, and whether that links procedure 1 to procedure 2.
walkthrough:
**What does burning sulfur give?**

Burning sulfur in excess oxygen gives sulfur dioxide, not sulfur trioxide directly. This is the starting point for both procedures.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2$$

**How can $\text{SO}_2$ become $\text{SO}_3$?**

$\text{SO}_2$ needs to be oxidised by gaining one more oxygen atom. Nitrogen dioxide, $\text{NO}_2$, can do this very readily.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{SO}_2 + \text{NO}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_3 + \text{NO}$$

**What happens when NO is added with excess oxygen?**

In procedure 1, $\text{NO}$ is added to a mixture that still contains excess $\text{O}_2$. $\text{NO}$ is easily oxidised by oxygen to make $\text{NO}_2$ in situ.

Chemical equation:
$$2\text{NO} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NO}_2$$

**Put the cycle together**

So procedure 2 supplies $\text{NO}_2$ directly to oxidise $\text{SO}_2$. Procedure 1 makes $\text{NO}_2$ from $\text{NO}$ plus the excess $\text{O}_2$, and then that $\text{NO}_2$ does the same oxidation. Both routes therefore produce some $\text{SO}_3$.

options.A: Correct. Procedure 2 works directly via $\text{SO}_2 + \text{NO}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_3 + \text{NO}$. Procedure 1 also works because the added $\text{NO}$ reacts with the excess $\text{O}_2$ to form $\text{NO}_2$, which then oxidises $\text{SO}_2$. This is the basis of the nitrogen oxides catalysed oxidation.
options.B: Incorrect. It is true that procedure 1 works, but procedure 2 also works. Students choosing this may forget that $\text{NO}_2$ directly oxidises $\text{SO}_2$ to $\text{SO}_3$.
options.C: Incorrect. It is true that procedure 2 works, but procedure 1 also works. Students choosing this often think $\text{NO}$ cannot oxidise $\text{SO}_2$, forgetting that $\text{NO}$ is first converted to $\text{NO}_2$ by the excess oxygen present.
options.D: Incorrect. Students choosing this often think only a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst (Contact process) can make $\text{SO}_3$. While that is the modern industrial method, nitrogen oxides also promote this oxidation.
